title: Building specialised care through clinical partnerships

contentHtml:
Nivam Orthopaedics recently partnered with Surya Hospitals to establish specialised orthopaedic centres in Mumbai. Dr Bhupendra S Avasthi, Founder, Chairman and Managing Director, Surya Hospitals, and Dr Nilen Shah, Founder, Nivam Orthopaedics, in an interview with Kalyani Sharma, discuss the rationale behind the partnership, plans to expand speciality care, and the role of dedicated clinical teams, technology and research in improving orthopaedic care

How does this partnership strengthen Surya’s positioning in women’s healthcare?

Dr Avasthi:A large proportion of orthopaedic conditions, particularly arthritis and joint problems, affect women. By adding specialised orthopaedic centres within our hospitals, we can offer more complete care to the same patient population we already serve for maternity, gynaecology and related needs.

Patients do not have to go to a separate facility for joint or spine care. They can access it within the same trusted ecosystem, supported by our multidisciplinary capabilities including intensive care and other specialties when required.

Why did Surya choose to partner with Nivam Orthopaedics rather than build orthopaedic services internally?

Dr Avasthi: We look for clinical teams that already have an established track record and a focused model of care. Dr Nilen Shah and Dr Manan Shah have developed a specialised approach to joint replacement and comprehensive orthopaedic care.

Rather than starting from scratch, we preferred to bring in a team that already has the clinical depth, systems and experience. This allows us to offer high-quality orthopaedic services more quickly while remaining true to Surya’s standards of patient-centric care.

At Surya Hospitals, we are people’s people — we believe in growing with the right partners who share our commitment to patients and clinical excellence.

What role will specialised centres such as Nivam Ortho play in Surya Hospitals’ expansion strategy?

Dr Avasthi: Surya has evolved from a hospital focused on pre-adolescent children to one providing care for women and children. While our Pune centre continues to focus on mother and childcare, our Mumbai operations have expanded to include a wider range of women’s healthcare needs.

Women may require care for conditions such as thyroid disorders, cancer and other medical issues beyond obstetrics and gynaecology. We wanted to build a more comprehensive model of care, including adult intensive care and other specialities. Orthopaedics is one of the first areas we have added through this partnership, we are pleased to work with a team that has an established track record and we have also started with the Cardiology.

Our approach to expansion is gradual. We want to consolidate our existing operations, identify the right clinical teams and ensure that each centre has the expertise needed to deliver quality care. This is a partnership in which the doctors and the hospital grow together.

With demand for specialised healthcare rising, how can hospitals balance clinical quality, operational efficiency and affordability?

Dr Avasthi: We have always tried to ensure that patients are not turned away simply because they cannot afford treatment. Over the years, we have supported families through the hospital, charitable trusts and other assistance wherever possible. A premature baby from a low-income family deserves the same opportunity for a healthy life as any other baby.

The expansion of health insurance has made treatment more accessible to many patients. However, there will still be families who need financial support, and we will continue to help wherever we can.

Affordability also depends on the way doctors practise. I value clinicians who maintain ethical standards and follow a consistent approach to their fees rather than charging differently based on a patient’s financial background. Clinical competence, sincerity and ethical practice must go together.

Dr Shah: Medical knowledge is a form of wealth that grows when it is shared and put to use. Restricting one’s practice to a particular class of patients also limits opportunities to learn and improve. Doctors need to acquire knowledge, share it with colleagues and help strengthen healthcare delivery across the country.

I have been involved in teaching for many years and have trained around 150 orthopaedic surgeons. Building teams through training and knowledge-sharing allows us to extend good clinical care to more patients.

There is a difference between saying that healthcare should be accessible and making it accessible in practice. Hospitals need to build affordability into their model of care, rather than treating it as an additional responsibility.

What are the key considerations when building a specialised orthopaedic care model within a multispeciality hospital network?

Dr Shah: The first consideration is whether the centre addresses a genuine clinical need. Musculoskeletal conditions, including arthritis, are common among women, so specialised orthopaedic care can complement a hospital network that already has a strong focus on women’s health.

The second consideration is access to the right infrastructure and expertise. Once a centre has the necessary equipment, instruments and trained teams, it can extend its services to a wider patient population.

I believe dedicated units focused on specific areas of medicine will play an increasingly important role in the development of hospital infrastructure. In our case, the advantage is that we can combine specialised orthopaedic services with the wider support of a multispeciality hospital, including cardiology, catheterisation laboratories and intensive care.

Most orthopaedic patients may not need these additional services, but they must be readily available when required. At the same time, a dedicated team can focus on orthopaedic care. When doctors, nurses and other staff work regularly within the same speciality, they develop the experience and skills needed to deliver consistent care.

How have advances in orthopaedic surgery improved patient outcomes?

Dr Shah: When I started practising, patients often stayed in hospital for two to three weeks after orthopaedic surgery. Today, some patients can return home on the same day, depending on the procedure and their clinical condition.

This change has been driven by improvements in pain management, anaesthesia, surgical techniques, implants and postoperative care. Minimally invasive approaches to knee and hip surgery have also contributed to recovery.

Robotic-assisted surgery is another development that can help surgeons position implants according to a planned surgical approach. These advances have changed both the surgical process and the way patients recover, although outcomes continue to depend on appropriate patient selection, clinical expertise and postoperative support.

As robotic-assisted surgery gains ground, what evidence should hospitals consider before investing in the technology?

Dr Shah: There is little doubt that robotic systems can help surgeons plan and execute implant positioning with greater precision. The more important question is whether that precision consistently translates into better clinical outcomes for patients.

Research has shown potential benefits, but the evidence does not conclusively establish superior clinical outcomes across all settings and patient groups. This remains an area of ongoing research and development.

Hospitals should therefore evaluate the technology carefully rather than assume that its availability automatically improves outcomes. At our centre, we want to offer robotic-assisted surgery while continuing to perform procedures without robotics where appropriate. We also intend to document our results systematically and compare outcomes so that our experience can contribute to the wider evidence base.

The objective should be to understand where the technology adds value, for which patients and under what circumstances.

Is clinical research in orthopaedics receiving enough attention in India?

Dr Shah: Clinical research is taking place in India, and Indian clinicians are publishing studies in international journals and presenting their findings at scientific forums. There is encouraging work in this area, although more needs to be done, particularly in strengthening basic research.

One of the priorities at Nivam Ortho will be systematic data collection, analysis and documentation. This will help us evaluate our clinical practice, understand outcomes and produce research that can inform our own decisions as well as those of other clinicians.

For specialised centres, research should not be separate from clinical practice. It should be part of the effort to improve the quality of care over time.

How do you see the role of partnerships like the one with Nivam Orthopaedics in the long-term growth of Surya Hospitals?

Dr Avasthi: Partnerships allow us to expand our clinical capabilities without losing focus on what we do best. At Surya, our foundation remains women and children’s healthcare. At the same time, we recognise that patients, especially women, often need care across multiple specialties over the course of their lives.

By working with specialised clinical teams such as Nivam Orthopaedics, we can offer a wider range of services within the same hospital ecosystem. This strengthens continuity of care and builds long-term trust with patients and families.

Our approach is not to expand in every direction at once. We prefer to identify the right partners, integrate them carefully into our system, and grow together. Over time, such collaborations help us create a more complete and sustainable model of care while remaining true to Surya’s core identity.
